name: Broken Oghibbeway
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.note: Extinct pidgin; Glottolog lists no references at all.

sources.citation: Rhodes, Richard A. 2008. Algonquian Trade Languages Revisited. Papers of the 40th Algonquian Conference (eds. K. S. Hele & J. R. Valentine), 358-369.
sources.note: Nothing. pp. 364-367 discuss Broken Oghibbeway from Nichols 1995 (word order SVO, Ottawa question words), quoting Nichols 1995:3 that his retranscriptions 'normalize toward Ojibwe pronunciations, ignoring, for the present, evidence of Menominee or other influence on the pronunciation of BOj' and that 'James's handwriting is difficult to read'. No stress/accent statement.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Broken Oghibbeway' (citing Nichols 1995:1-2 and Bakker 2003:16); Glottolog 5.x languoid page brok1252 (no references listed).
sources.note: Nothing on phonology or stress; identifies the sole attestation as Edwin James's 1820s notes from Prairie du Chien, vocabulary 'drawn from the Ottawa dialect of Ojibwe with a few words from the Fox language'.

sources.citation: Bakker, Peter. 1994. Is John Long's Chippeway (1791) an Ojibwa Pidgin? Papers of the 25th Algonquian Conference (ed. W. Cowan), 14-31. Ottawa: Carleton University.
sources.note: Nothing. Section 7 'Broken Oghibbeway (Nichols 1992)', pp. 29-30, is a second-hand summary of Nichols's 1992 Algonquian Conference paper: subject prefixes, plural suffixes, tense prefixes retained; no negative suffix, obviative, object inflection or conjunct; invariable stems. No phonology, no stress/accent remark.

sources.citation: Nichols, John D. 1995. The Ojibwe verb in "Broken Oghibbeway." Amsterdam Creole Studies 12: 1-18. Amsterdam: Instituut voor Algemene Taalwetenschap, Universiteit van Amsterdam.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only first-hand linguistic description of the pidgin (from the Edwin James manuscript); pp. 1-3 describe the source and transcription practice and would settle whether James marked accent at all and whether Nichols says anything about pronunciation/prosody (expected: silent on stress).

sources.citation: Bakker, Peter. 2003. Pidgin inflectional morphology and its implications for creole morphology. In G. Booij & J. van Marle (eds.), Yearbook of Morphology 2002, 3-33. Dordrecht: Kluwer.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Most-cited secondary treatment of Broken Oghibbeway structure; would confirm that published discussion is confined to morphology (low chance of any prosodic remark).
